Beállítom Az Európai Központi Bank (EKB) Kormányzótanácsa csütörtöki ülésén a piaci várakozásokkal összhangban 25 bázisponttal emelte a három irányadó eurókamat szintjét, írja az MTI. A döntés értelmében szeptember 16-tól a betéti rendelkezésre állás kamatlába 2,25 százalékról 2,50 százalékra, az irányadó refinanszírozási műveletek kamatlába 2,40 százalékról 2,65 százalékra, az aktív oldali rendelkezésre állás kamatlába pedig 2,65 százalékról 2,90 százalékra emelkedik. A döntés megfelelt a piaci várakozásoknak. A kormányzótanács előző, júliusi kamatdöntő ülésén változatlanul hagyta a három irányadó eurókamat szintjét, ugyancsak összhangban a piaci várakozásokkal, júniusban 25 bázisponttal emelte azokat. Ezt megelőzően legutóbb tavaly júniusban változtatott a kamatszinteken, akkor 25 bázisponttal csökkentette a három irányadó eurókamatot. Ezzel szemben a Magyar Nemzeti Bank idén nyáron minikamatvágási ciklusba kezdett a kedvező külső körülmények miatt (pl. erős forint, alacsony infláció), ennek értelmében augusztusban 5,5 százalékra csökkentette az irányadó alapkamatot. A szakértők ekkor azt mondták, nagy az esély arra, hogy a ciklus szeptemberben folytatódjon. Bár a külső környezet ugyan romlott – világszerte emelkednek a hosszú hozamok, és nőttek az energiaár- és geopolitikai kockázatok – ez viszont a magas magyar reálkamat mellett nem tántorította el a jegybankot. Varga Mihály jegybankelnök ekkor azt mondta, ősszel még meglátják, engedi-e a világgazdasági helyzet (pl. az olajárak alakulása) a folytatást, így ezt majd a friss inflációs jelentés ismeretében dönti el a Monetáris Tanács. A magyar jegybank szeptemberi döntésében valószínűleg az EKB mostani lépését is mérlegelni fogják. Az EKB a csütörtöki döntés indoklásában kiemelte: a közel-keleti konfliktus továbbra is inflációs nyomást okoz, az infláció várhatóan hosszabb ideig jóval az EKB célja felett marad, elkötelezett amellett, hogy olyan monetáris politikát folytasson, amivel az inflációt középtávon a 2 százalékos célján stabilizálják. Photograph: Jeff Swensen/Getty Images The Stakes 2026 US midterm elections 2026 Analysis A rare red line in deeply cynical times Lauren Gambino It’s been a particularly brutal cycle for attack ads, but voters are responding with humanity. Plus: on the campaign trail with a Democrat in Kansas This was originally published in the Stakes 2026, a newsletter about the midterm elections. Sign up to get it in your inbox Fri 30 Oct 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 07.13 EDT Share There’s a campaign moment I can’t stop thinking about. It happened shortly after the campaign of Vivek Ramaswamy , the Republican nominee for governor of Ohio, released a shocking attack ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton. In the ad, as many readers will know by now, Acton’s mother accuses her daughter of lying and tells Ohioans not to vote for her. Acton, 60, says she has not spoken to her mother since she was 12, when she and her brother were removed from their mother’s custody after their stepfather was arrested and charged with raping her. Acton says she last saw her mother at the courthouse, where her mother came to support her husband as her daughter testified against him. The moment that captured my attention took place at a campaign event on a farm in Wharton, Ohio , and it was much less newsy. Acton was speaking to a group of supporters and a woman asked: “Can I give you a hug?” “Of course you can,” the candidate replied, walking over and allowing herself to be embraced. After watching the ad, the woman told Acton: “All I wanted to do was cry and hug you and tell you it’ll be OK.” It was a small moment of humanity in what has otherwise been a particularly vicious campaign season, even by the standards of the Trump era. After weeks of wondering ‘how much lower can they go’, particularly on the right, Ramaswamy pulled out a shovel and dug deeper. View image in fullscreen Campaign signs outside the Lake county board of elections in Painesville, Ohio, on Monday. Photograph: Shannon Stapleton/Reuters In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate, has faced a barrage of ads attacking his religion (he is Muslim) and claiming, baselessly, that he has ties to Islamic terrorist organizations. As Donald Trump barnstorms the country trying to salvage Republicans’ majorities in Congress, he has hurled Islamophobic invectives at El-Sayed. In Texas, the Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton and his allies have pumped out controversial ads – many of them AI-generated – that attack his opponent James Talarico as effeminate and misstate his position on transgender rights. JD Vance doubled down on that line of attack, baselessly musing that Talarico was gay. Perhaps unsurprisingly, both Trump and Vance have defended Ramaswamy’s ad. “ Stop whining ,” the vice-president told Republicans who had called for the ad to come down. Ramaswamy, a billionaire entrepreneur who has embraced the president’s never-back-down, politics-as-bloodsport ethos, was defiant. Many Republicans, including the state’s outgoing governor, Mike DeWine, have condemned the ad alongside Acton. “It’s wrong to run this ad,” said DeWine, who has endorsed Ramaswamy. On Thursday, amid mounting pressure and polling that found the ad backfiring, Ramaswamy said that his campaign had discontinued it. Politics has never been for the faint of heart. Attack ads have long been a tool of political combat. In 1964, Lyndon Johnson’s presidential campaign pulled the so-called “Daisy” ad from TV amid fierce public criticism over its suggestion that the Republican nominee, Barry Goldwater, would wage nuclear war if elected. The “Daisy” ad seems almost quaint now, from the vantage point of 2026, a year in which the US president threatened to “annihilate” Iran in a speech before the United Nations general assembly. Trump has crossed so many red lines since he emerged as a presidential candidate in 2015 – gleefully breaking political, legal and constitutional norms – that it can be hard to tell what the rules of engagement are any more. He has mocked world leaders , flattered dictators , disparaged political opponents as the “ enemy within ”, encouraged violence against protesters, called a female journalist “ piggy ”, declared that undocumented immigrants were “ poisoning the blood ” of the country, and on and on . So it took me by surprise that the Ramaswamy ad was met with such strong bipartisan condemnation – the rare red line in deeply cynical times. The ruthless ad aired in Ohio, a one-time presidential battleground that has shifted toward Republicans in recent election cycles but is home this year to several competitive races. Will the ad have a blast radius that hurts other Republicans in the state, like Jon Husted, the incumbent Ohio senator whose posterior Trump can’t stop raving about ? View image in fullscreen Amy Acton making a campaign stop in Youngstown, Ohio. Photograph: Shannon Stapleton/Reuters Acton must have known when she decided to run that the campaign would be ugly. She first rose to prominence in early 2020 as the director of the Ohio department of health. She became an early face of the pandemic response and, in the beginning, was roundly praised for her clearly communicated daily briefings, inspiring bobblehead dolls and little girls’ Halloween costumes. But as backlash brewed against the state’s lockdown measures, she also became a high-profile target of armed protests outside her home, antisemitic slurs (Acton is Jewish) and misinformation campaigns. At a campaign event earlier this fall, an armed man was arrested after lunging at Acton as she spoke at a county fair. She was not injured, and Acton, a physician, stayed on site to treat one of the onlookers injured in the episode. For many disgusted voters in Ohio, the choice on Tuesday is now between a woman who at 12 took the stand in court to testify against her mother’s husband – the man charged with raping her, while her mother stood by his side – and a man who allowed that dark story to be twisted into a political attack ad. Maybe after Tuesday, it’s Ramaswamy who will need consoling. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly, plus breaking news alerts Sign up to The Stakes 2026 A weekly guide to what really matters in the US midterms, plus breaking news alerts. after newsletter promotion Meet the candidate: Adam Hamilton View image in fullscreen Adam Hamilton at a campaign rally in Emporia, Kansas, this week. Photograph: Mark Reinstein/Shutterstock Kansas hasn’t elected a Democrat to the US Senate in nearly 100 years. Adam Hamilton is running to change that. Hamilton, a United Methodist pastor, is challenging the Republican incumbent, Senator Roger Marshall, who was elected in 2020. My colleague, Rachel Leingang , was recently in the unexpected battleground state to catch Hamilton on the campaign trail. Hamilton, a former Republican who had considered running as an independent, regularly points to one of his state’s most famous residents: Dorothy from The Wizard of Oz. Recalling a visit he made to Liberal, Kansas, and its Oz museum, he asks the audience to recall what Dorothy’s companions on her journey need. The lion needed courage, the scarecrow a brain and the tin man a heart. Washington needs more of all three, he likes to say, and he can deliver it. Read more: Kansas Democrat’s pitch to voters amid historic Senate bid: ‘I’m gonna just fight like hell’ 📣 Quoted We’re watching a bit of a political revolution play out in slow motion. – Stan Barnes, a political consultant and former Republican state senator in Arizona, referring to his party’s eroding support in the suburbs around Maricopa county, which has powered a slate of Democratic victories in the years since Trump was first elected to the White House This year, Arizona Democrats believe they can finally flip congressional district 1, where Democrat Amish Shah – an emergency room doctor who narrowly lost the seat in 2024 – and Republican Jay Feely – a former National Football League kicker backed by Donald Trump – are battling for the House seat left open by Republican congressman David Schweikert. Read more: ‘A revolution in slow motion’: is Arizona’s wealthiest district finally done with Trump? Photograph: Peter Foley/Bloomberg via Getty Images US news Analysis Maurene Comey ruling offers hope of check on Trump’s assault on rule of law Victoria Bekiempis in New York Legal experts welcome judge’s rejection of firing of James Comey’s daughter prosecutor but warn an appeal is likely Sat 31 Oct 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 11.02 EDT Share A recent legal ruling against an effort to fire the star-prosecutor daughter of a former FBI chief targeted by Donald Trump could send a strong message about politicized firings – and influence other judges weighing similar cases, legal veterans said. Judge Jesse Furman ruled this week that the Department of Justice’s firing of assistant US attorney Maurene Comey without cause was unlawful. Comey, the daughter of former FBI director James Comey, successfully litigated numerous high-profile cases during her tenure at the southern district of New York, including guilty verdicts against Ghislaine Maxwell and Sean “Diddy” Combs. “It looks as if Judge Furman has completely vindicated her and rejected just about all of the arguments made by the government,” said Carl Tobias, Williams chair at the University of Richmond School of Law. “And so it’s really important to have this because of the way she was essentially summarily fired, and so it sets a valuable precedent.” Maurene Comey was illegally fired as federal prosecutor, judge rules Read more The Department of Justice, which fired her without cause, had argued thatarticle II of the US constitution, which defines presidential power, imbued Trump and his attorney general with a right to fire line prosecutors – who are not political appointees. But Furman this week rejected the department’s position, ruling Comey’s firing was not greenlighted under any law and in fact, violated the Civil Service Reform Act. View image in fullscreen Maurene Comey, then an assistant US attorney, points at Ghislaine Maxwell, far left, while she presents the rebuttal for the prosecution during Maxwell’s sex-trafficking trial in New York in 2021. Photograph: Elizabeth Williams/AP The justice department’s claim “flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent”, Furman said. “It is also without merit. Indeed, to accept Defendants’ argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation’s constitutional system.” For legal observers, Furman’s decision is cause for optimism – even if optimism of the cautious sort – amid the Trump administration’s alleged repeated attacks on the rule of law. While one judicial opinion does not a panacea make, they said, such a ruling can send a strong message and be considered by other judges weighing similar cases. “One thing I would caution is that it’s very clear the government will appeal this,” Tobias said. The justice department would do this via the second circuit court of appeals. “I expect that Furman would be affirmed by that court, and then I assume the administration would then appeal to the US supreme court,” he added. Then, it would up to the US supreme court to decide whether they even want to hear the case – and if they decline, the lower appeals court decision would stand. “You are seeing the courts step up and stop and prevent the administration when they are violating the rule of law,” said Neama Rahmani, founder of West Coast Trial Lawyers and a former federal prosecutor. Just this Monday, Los Angeles federal court judge David Carter rejected Trump’s attempt to set aside 20,000 ballots in California, Rahmani noted. “Whether it’s the supreme court and birthright citizenship, or even individual cases like this, there have been limited, I would say, rulings by the court that have limited what President Trump can do.” Like Tobias, Rahmani said the justice department can fight federal district and appeals court decisions. And, this kind of case does contain legal issues that might pique the supreme court’s interest – especially if different federal appeals courts were to reach different conclusions. If the supreme court did decide to hear arguments on Comey’s case, it would by no means guarantee a check on Trump’s power. “There are a lot of the justices on the supreme court that really don’t believe there should be much of any restrictions on what the president can do,” Rahmani said. “So this is far from the silver bullet.” For now, though, Furman’s decision can prove influential. “The decision can be used by other folks who do believe that they were terminated lawfully,” Rahmani said, adding, “It is not binding at all, but it’s certainly something that judges look to with similar or exact same facts.” Elizabeth Wolstein, a partner at Schlam Stone & Dolan LLP and former Manhattan federal prosecutor in the civil division, said that a judge’s decision in one case could potentially affect how other judges’ weigh similar issues. “It doesn’t have any binding effect on another judge, even in the same district, as opposed to how a second circuit or US supreme court case would be binding,” Wolstein said. But, “if it’s well reasoned and persuasive, it is definitely going to be persuasive to another judge faced with a similar issue.” Comey filed suit over her ouster in September 2025. Comey said she neither received notice nor explanation of her firing. Instead, Comey on 16 July 2025 got a letter that stated “your employment with the Department of Justice is hereby terminated, and you are removed from federal service effective immediately.” When Comey asked the then Manhattan US attorney, Jay Clayton, about this notice, he allegedly said “all I can say is it came from Washington. I can’t tell you anything else,” per court papers. The Department of Justice has said Comey’s firing was directed by the former US attorney general Pam Bondi and subsequently “ratified” by her successor, Todd Blanche. Comey’s lawyers and critics of the US president have claimed that she was fired because her father is longtime Trump foe James Comey. Trump’s justice department has repeatedly tried prosecuting James Comey, this week making public its third case against him; one prior proceeding was dismissed, another is pending. The department had defended the idea that someone’s familial relations could be considered in termination proceedings. Maurene Comey’s legal team viewed Furman’s ruling as a positive development in protecting the rule of law. Comey’s attorneys are Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron and Deepa Vanamali at Clarick Gueron Reisbaum, as well as Margaret Donovan at Koskoff Koskoff & Bieder. “The Court’s decision is a complete rejection of this administration’s sweeping claim to unchecked executive power, and it demonstrates that our constitutional system of checks and balances is alive and well,” the team said in a statement. The justice department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Furman’s decision or claims of politically driven firings. In a statement, the White House rejected allegations that Trump’s justice department is trying to punish opponents. “Unlike Joe Biden, President Trump has not weaponized the Department of Justice against his political foes. The Department is focused on restoring law and order and keeping Americans safe,” Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement. “The results speak for themselves: Under President Trump, we have seen the largest decrease in violent crime in American history.” Explore more on these topics US news Trump administration US justice system analysis Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.politico.eu/article/ex-labou.text: LONDON — A former Labour MP who was suspended from the party following allegations of sexual harassment has joined Plaid Cymru, the ruling party in Wales. Geraint Davies made the announcement on the news website Nation Cymru, where he claimed that he was forced out as an MP because of “local rivalries and disobeying Keir Starmer’s orders to speaking [sic] out against killings in Gaza.” He described allegations of sexual misconduct against him as “untrue anonymous hearsay in the media.” Advertisement Advertisement In 2023, five women alleged that Davies, a former Commons select committee chair, subjected them to unwanted sexual attention, both physical and verbal, after coming into contact with them through his work as an MP. Davies had the whip suspended as a Labour MP immediately after the allegations were made public but remained a member of the party until 2025. When the claims against Davies were first reported by POLITICO, he said he did not “recognize” them, adding: “If I have inadvertently caused offence to anyone, then I am naturally sorry.” In these instances, the women had raised concerns about his behavior informally but had not complained in writing. At least two women later filed official complaints with the Labour Party, resulting in an investigation lasting more than a year. Davies was not eligible to stand as a candidate in the 2024 election because he was suspended, and quit the party ahead of a planned hearing on his conduct in 2025. As a result, the hearing never went ahead. The former MP for Swansea West argued in the article published Thursday that the party engineered his removal as a candidate for factional reasons. “I was made to wait 23 weeks without any complaints. When complaints were made, they were ‘to support other women’ who had not made any complaints. None were reported to Parliament,” he said. Advertisement Advertisement Two women who previously made allegations against Davies, and were granted anonymity to protect their privacy, contacted POLITICO on Friday to object to his statement to Nation Cymru. One, a sitting Labour MP first elected in 2015, said she had entered a formal complaint with the party to raise an allegation of unwanted touching. “Having been touched by Geraint against my wishes, I can say the allegations of sexual harassment are more than hearsay. Whilst I can’t speak for other women’s experiences, I know the way he touched me left me deeply upset and unsettled and I spent most of the years we were both MPs trying to put as much physical distance between us as was possible,” she said. A second woman said: “As someone who experienced this behaviour firsthand, I know that these claims are not hearsay. Women don’t come forward because of exactly this kind of platform and response.” A Labour Party spokesperson said: “All complaints are assessed thoroughly in line with our rules and procedures. To protect the confidentiality of the complainants, we do not provide information about specific allegations made.” They added: “It is categorically untrue to suggest that the fact Mr Davies was not re-selected as a Labour candidate was unconnected to the serious allegations made about his conduct.” A spokesperson for Plaid Cymru, the Welsh nationalist party, said: “Plaid Cymru treats all complaints of sexual harassment and abuse with the utmost seriousness. Every concern raised is taken seriously, and allegations are considered fairly and thoroughly, taking into account all available evidence. We encourage anyone who has experienced or witnessed inappropriate behaviour to come forward, so that concerns can be properly investigated and appropriate action taken.” Davies did not respond to a request for comment.
